content: Linaclotide is indicated for the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) at a dosage of 290 mcg taken orally once daily. For chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC), the recommended dosage is 145 mcg taken orally once daily, although a lower dose of 72 mcg may be used depending on the individual patient’s presentation. In pediatric patients aged 6 to 17 years with functional constipation (FC), the recommended dosage is 72 mcg taken orally once daily. Hypersensitivity reactions to linaclotide may include anaphylaxis, angioedema, and skin rashes such as hives or urticaria. Gastrointestinal side effects may include hematochezia (blood in stool), nausea, and rectal bleeding. Linaclotide is contraindicated in patients under 2 years of age due to the risk of severe dehydration and in individuals with known or suspected mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction. Linaclotide and its active metabolite are minimally absorbed systemically after oral administration. However, there is insufficient data on the use of linaclotide in pregnant women to determine any drug-associated risks for major birth defects or miscarriage. Studies have shown that linaclotide and its active metabolite are not detectable in the milk of lactating women, and plasma concentrations of the drug and its metabolite are below the limit of quantification in adults after multiple doses. Consequently, maternal use of linaclotide is not expected to expose breastfed infants to the drug or its active metabolite. There is no information on the effects of linaclotide on milk production. When considering linaclotide use during breastfeeding, healthcare providers should weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Linaclotide is a guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) agonist. Activation of GC-C on the luminal surface of intestinal epithelial cells increases cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), leading to enhanced anion secretion, fluid secretion, and accelerated intestinal transit. The drug appears to act locally within the gastrointestinal tract rather than systemically. Elevation of intracellular cGMP stimulates the secretion of chloride and bicarbonate into the intestinal lumen, primarily through activation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) ion channel, resulting in increased intestinal fluid and faster transit. Linaclotide undergoes minimal systemic absorption, and plasma concentrations of the drug and its active metabolite are below the limit of quantification after oral doses of 145 mcg or 290 mcg. The drug is metabolized within the gastrointestinal tract to its principal active metabolite by the removal of the terminal tyrosine moiety. Both linaclotide and its metabolite are proteolytically degraded within the intestinal lumen into smaller peptides and naturally occurring amino acids. Approximately 3-5% of the parent compound is excreted in the feces, along with nearly 100% of the active metabolite. Linaclotide should be taken on an empty stomach at least 30 minutes before the first meal of the day, ideally at the same time each day. The capsule should be swallowed whole and not chewed or crushed. The medication should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with permissible temperature excursions between 15-30°C (59-86°F). It must be kept in its original container to protect it from moisture, and the desiccant should not be removed.
